name: Ingrown hair treatments (salicylic, tend skin)

lead: These products aim to cut down razor bumps and ingrown hairs so the beard area, neck and other shaved skin look clearer and smoother. Curly-haired people are most affected.

Exfoliating acids loosen dead skin that can trap hairs and reduce inflammation, while the underlying cause is cut hair curling back into the skin. Dermatology sources list salicylic and glycolic acid peels and retinoids as options; branded consumer products have not been individually studied.

paras: People apply a salicylic-acid lotion or pad to shaved areas after shaving and between shaves. It is often combined with gentler shaving habits or letting hair grow longer.
Acids can irritate skin. Severe or recurrent cases can cause scarring or infection, and sources advise medical care when lesions persist or become infected.

web.title: Ingrown hair treatments (salicylic, tend skin) — Grokipedia

chain: Acid loosens dead skin over hairs
angle.text: Salicylic-acid after-shave products loosen the dead skin over trapped hairs so they release, leaving fewer razor bumps and clearer skin, especially on the beard area with curly hair. The condition is well documented, though branded products are not individually studied.

lead: Ingrown hair treatments are topical products, often containing salicylic acid, marketed to reduce bumps and irritation where shaved hairs curl back into the skin. Ingrown hairs, called pseudofolliculitis barbae in the beard area, are common after shaving, especially in people with tightly curled hair.[1][1]

Clinical sources list salicylic acid and glycolic acid peels and tretinoin among dermatology treatments, and note that letting hair grow is the simplest approach.[2] Studies of branded consumer products such as Tend Skin were not found.
infobox: Salicylic acid, glycolic acid, retinoids (Rx), benzoyl peroxide
High among those with curly hair who shave

paras: An ingrown hair forms when a cut hair curls back into or grows sideways into the skin, acting as a foreign body and causing inflammatory bumps.[1][3] Curly hair is a major risk factor, and a keratin gene variant has been linked to the condition.[2] The condition is particularly frequent among Black men who shave, and a 1988 review called it distressing though not medically serious, with no cure and individualized treatment.[3]

Wikipedia lists salicylic acid peels, glycolic acid peels, nightly tretinoin, antibiotics, benzoyl peroxide, laser hair removal and electrolysis, and states that stopping shaving for three to four weeks lets most lesions subside.[2] Prevention advice includes using a sharp single-blade razor, shaving with the grain, softening the beard, and keeping hair at a short length with a trimmer.[2] Grokipedia describes similar measures.[1]
Salicylic-acid lotions and similar products are discussed in grooming communities as after-shave steps for bumps. No citable community material was available.
No studies found of consumer salicylic-acid ingrown hair products specifically. Related literature includes reviews of pseudofolliculitis barbae pathogenesis and treatment.[4][5]
